title: My uncle will pay RM80,000 if I buy a landed home. Should I take it?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #189 | UNCLE DONATE MONEY TO BUY PROPERTY
excerpt: A 32-year-old father renting in Ampang is offered RM80,000 by his uncle, but only for a landed home to live in. Sean shows the real cash needed and why he would politely decline.

qa.asker: H, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: H is 32, married with a two-year-old, earns RM6,500 a month and his wife about RM4,500. They rent a 900 sq ft unit in Ampang and have RM50,000 in ASB as an emergency fund. He owns one investment unit, completed in 2019, that costs him about RM400 a month above its rent. His uncle has offered up to RM80,000 for the down payment on a RM700,000 to RM800,000 landed home, but only for his own stay, with instalments of RM3,500 to RM4,500.
qa.question: Should he accept and buy a landed home now, or keep renting and build investment properties first as planned?
qa.quote: My first property is not my only property.
qa.answer: Sean would decline. RM80,000 doesn't come close to covering a landed home, which would eat most of his income and block his loan eligibility for investments. Keep renting, keep building investment properties, and upgrade to a landed home in about ten years with his own money.

reasons.title: The real cash needed is far more than RM80,000
reasons.body: A RM700,000 subsale needs about 18% up front, roughly RM126,000 for the down payment, stamp duty and fees, plus at least RM50,000 to make it livable. He would still need about RM100,000 of his own.

reasons.title: It would leave no room for shocks
reasons.body: With RM3,500 to RM4,500 going on the loan before his car, insurance and family costs, every rate rise or family emergency would be stressful.

reasons.title: His loan eligibility would be tied up
reasons.body: A RM700,000 loan on his credit record would use up his debt service ratio, ending the plan of buying investment units whose rent eventually pays for his home.

reasons.title: A small monthly top-up can be acceptable
reasons.body: Paying RM400 a month still builds equity. Before selling his investment unit, check its market value against what he owes, and consider refreshing it to raise the rent.

actions: Work out the full cash needed for a landed home, including fees and renovation.
Check what is still owed on the investment unit and its current market value before selling.
Consider small improvements to raise its rent instead.
Plan to upgrade to a landed home once his investments and income can carry it.
Ask why the offer is only for a landed home, and what may be expected in return.
qa.caveat: If his only goal is one family home and he accepts five to ten years of tight finances, taking the gift is reasonable. Family dynamics differ, and Sean admits his preference for independence is personal.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #189. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in September 2022. Sean says he, like the viewer, is a client of FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase company.
